opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think mentorship is one of the most underrated variables when people choose where to do research. People obsess over the prestige of the institution, or whether the topic sounds exciting, and those matter, but the thing that most determines how fast you grow is often who's giving you feedback and how often.

The first thing I'd look for is just *time*. A brilliant, famous advisor who sees you for 30 minutes once a month is often worse than a less famous but engaged mentor you talk to a couple of times a week. Research skill is largely tacit: knowing when to abandon an idea, when to push through, what a good experiment looks like, when you're fooling yourself. You mostly pick that up through tight feedback loops on your actual work, not abstract advice. So I'd literally ask: how often will we meet? Who do I go to when I'm stuck on a Tuesday afternoon?

Second, I'd talk to their current and former students or team members, ideally away from the mentor. Are people happy? Do they feel they've grown? Do they publish, and are their papers actually theirs, or are they executing someone else's vision? Did people leave burned out? You get much more honest signal this way than from a mentor's self-description.

Third, I'd look at whether their research taste is something you want to absorb. You'll end up inheriting a lot of your mentor's instincts about what's important and what counts as a convincing result. If their work doesn't excite you, or you think their standards of evidence are sloppy, that's a real cost even if they're very supportive.

Fourth, fit in style. Some people thrive with lots of structure, being told "here's a well-scoped project, go run these experiments." Others want freedom and find that stifling. Early on, I think most people underestimate how much they benefit from structure and concrete direction. Picking your own research direction well is a skill that takes time to build, and being thrown into the deep end can mean a year spinning your wheels.

On PhD versus industry specifically: industry teams can be great here because you're often surrounded by several experienced people, not just one advisor, and there's a lot of informal learning from colleagues. But that depends heavily on the team. Some industry roles are more engineering-heavy with less investment in your development as a researcher, so the same questions apply: who will actually spend time with you, and what happened to the last few people in your seat?

And finally, don't rely on a single mentor. Even in a good setup, I'd encourage people to build a broader network of people they can get feedback from: collaborators, people in adjacent groups, folks online. A lot of my own growth came from just asking people smarter than me to look at my work and tell me what was wrong with it.

fable-5.1.text:
Neel Nanda: So I think the thing I care about most is whether the mentor is actually going to spend time with you, and whether that time is going to be high quality. There's a huge amount of variance here. Some PhD supervisors meet their students for an hour a week and give really detailed, engaged feedback on their ideas. Others have twenty students, are travelling constantly, and you're lucky to get a vague email once a month. And the label "PhD" or "industry team" tells you almost nothing about which of those you're going to get. You really have to ask the specific people.

The second thing I'd look for is taste. Research is mostly about making a long sequence of judgement calls: which problem to work on, which experiment to run first, when to abandon a direction, when a result is actually interesting versus just a curiosity. Most of what a good mentor gives you is calibration on those calls. So I'd want someone whose own research I actually admire, who has a track record of picking problems that turned out to matter, and ideally who can articulate why they made the choices they made rather than just having gotten lucky.

A third thing, which I think is underrated, is whether the mentor is going to let you be wrong in a productive way. Early on you want fairly tight feedback loops, where someone catches you before you spend three months on a dead end. But over time you want the scaffolding to come off, so you can develop your own judgement. The best mentors I've seen are pretty deliberate about that transition. The worst ones either micromanage forever, or throw you in the deep end on day one and call it independence.

And then practically, I'd ask: how often will we actually talk? Will you read my drafts? Will you look at my experimental results, or just the write-up? Who else on the team will I learn from? Because in a good industry team a lot of the mentorship is diffuse, it comes from pairing with other researchers, from code review, from arguing about results in a group channel. Whereas in a PhD it can be much more dependent on one person, which is higher variance in both directions.

Honestly, if I had to pick one thing, I'd go and talk to current and former students or reports of that person, and ask them directly how much time they got and whether it was useful. People are surprisingly candid about this, and it's far more informative than anything the mentor will tell you themselves.

r002.rationale: It says some supervisors have many students and little time, but does not connect this to famous PhD supervisors.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest thing is whether you’ll get useful feedback from someone who actually has time for you. It’s easy to focus on how impressive an adviser is as a researcher, but that’s a different question from whether they’ll be a good mentor for you.

I’d talk to their current students or junior researchers and ask quite concrete questions: How often do you meet? When you’re stuck, what happens? Do they help you work out which questions are worth pursuing? Can you bring them a half-formed idea and get a useful conversation out of it?

A lot of learning to do research is developing judgement. What’s a tractable problem? What would constitute evidence that your hypothesis is wrong? When should you keep pushing, and when should you move on? You want someone who helps you understand how they make those decisions, and gradually helps you make them yourself.

And I’d look at the wider team. Are there people you can ask basic questions without feeling embarrassed? Do people discuss their work and give each other feedback? Your official supervisor is only one part of the environment you’ll actually be learning in.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes an adviser’s ability as a researcher from whether they will be a good mentor.

r002.rationale: It says a mentor should have time for you, but does not connect limited time to famous PhD supervisors providing poor mentorship.

r003.rationale: It does not say that developing team members into strong researchers serves the manager’s own interests.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss differences in research autonomy across industry teams.

r005.rationale: It does not compare how easily engineering skills are learned in industry versus during a PhD.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: will this person actually help me become a better researcher? That’s different from whether they’re a great researcher themselves, or whether the institution is prestigious.

I’d want someone who has time for me, who’s excited about the questions I want to work on, and who can give concrete feedback. If I’m stuck, can they help me figure out why? If I have an idea, can they explain what’s promising about it and what would make it fail? And can they help me develop the judgment to answer those questions myself?

One of the best ways to assess that is to talk to people they’ve mentored, ideally including people who struggled. Ask what the day-to-day relationship actually looks like: how often they meet, what happens when a project isn’t working, and how much useful feedback they get. I’d put a lot more weight on those answers than on a vague promise of excellent mentorship.
